S1 · TrafficCold CalendarLive Session · ChallengeEmailSend 8–12 days before the session, Tue–Thu; test evening sends in the recipient's time zone.

Cold Calendar Invite, Long Form

A full invite body that carries the whole pitch: timing hook, what's changed, what they'll leave with, who it's for, who hosts, and how to reply.

Best example for: High-volume cold calendar sends where the invite has to sell the session on its own, with no email around it

S1 · TrafficCold CalendarLive Session · ChallengeEmailOne send 8–12 days out, Tue–Thu morning local; optional two-line follow-up four days later, then stop.

Cold Calendar Invite, Short Form

A 40–70 word invite that reads like an agenda a colleague forwarded: no claims, a named host, the link low and a consequence-free exit.

Best example for: Senior, time-poor buyers who distrust vendors, where brevity and a named human are the credibility signal

S1 · TrafficCold CalendarLive Session · ChallengeSchema

Calendar Invite Title Rubric

Score candidate titles on five weighted criteria so the one that renders its hook at 24 characters wins, not the one that sounds best in a meeting.

Best example for: Choosing an invite title that survives mobile truncation before you spend a list on it

S1 · TrafficCold EmailAll MechanismsEmail

Cold Email, Honest-Pitch Opener

Disarm the reader by naming the pitch in line one, then make it a pitch for a session, not for a product.

Best example for: Skeptical buyers who have been over-pitched, where admitting the pitch up front earns the second sentence

S1 · TrafficCold EmailAll MechanismsEmail

Cold Email, News Hook

Anchor the invite in a real, recent headline, then bridge from the headline to the session in two sentences.

Best example for: Refreshing a tired cold list with a timely angle when a public story in your category breaks

S1 · TrafficCold EmailAll MechanismsSequenceDay 0 · 3 · 7

Cold Email, Contrast Story (3 Emails)

Open with two peers who look identical on paper but got different outcomes, reveal the variable, and invite them to the session that teaches it.

Best example for: Status-driven buyers who benchmark themselves against peers, where 'same inputs, different outcome' creates the itch

S1 · TrafficCold EmailAll MechanismsSchema

Cold Email Tone Matrix (8 Tones)

The same session invite written in eight tones, each with its own subject pattern, opening move and CTA verb, so a list can be split by tone.

Best example for: Split-testing voice rather than offer: one invite, eight registers, so you learn which tone your list answers

S1 · TrafficCold EmailAll MechanismsSequenceDay 0 · 4 · 8

Cold Email, Meme Pattern Interrupt (3 Emails)

Lead with a personalised meme image and almost no copy, then deliver the substance in the reply, then close the loop.

Best example for: Technical buyers drowning in polished vendor mail, where one deliberately unprofessional image earns the open and the reply

Best example for: Teams exhibiting or attending an in-person event whose attendee list overlaps the ICP

A 300-character connection note plus four post-accept messages that move from a question, to free value, to a self-serve resource, to one ask.

Best example for: Cold prospects with no prior relationship, where the connection note has to buy the accept and nothing else

S1 · TrafficLinkedIn OutreachAll MechanismsScriptNote · Day 0 · 4 after accept

LinkedIn Case-Study Connection DM

A connection note that admits the category sounds dull, offers one specific case instead, and makes declining feel fine; then delivers the case and the session.

Best example for: Owner-operators who ignore category claims but will accept to see one concrete before-and-after

S1 · TrafficCold EmailAll MechanismsSchema

Sending-Domain Fleet Plan

One row per sending mailbox: domain, persona, purpose, warm-up, authentication, daily caps and status, so capacity and risk are visible at a glance.

Best example for: Planning mailbox and domain capacity before a cold email or calendar programme, so volume never burns the primary domain

S1 · TrafficSocial ContentAll MechanismsPostOne per week at most, alternating with story and news posts; retire a resource once comments slow

Comment-to-Get Resource Post

Offer a free tool or checklist in exchange for a connection and a one-word comment, so every taker is a warm, reachable ICP role.

Best example for: Growing the host's network with exactly the right people while handing out a genuinely useful free tool

S1 · TrafficSocial ContentAll MechanismsWorkflowOne recording in, 5–10 posts out; batch weekly

AI Content Prompt Pack

Five chained prompts that turn one recording into a batch of posts: find the segments, then write story, carousel, news and case-study posts in the host's voice.

Best example for: Teams that record sessions, calls and interviews and want a week of on-voice posts from each recording

One document that lets any writer, or any model, produce a post the host would sign without edits: who they are, who they write for, how they sound and what they never say.

Best example for: Anyone ghostwriting for a founder whose credibility is the whole asset, especially in regulated or technical markets

S1 · TrafficFoundationsAll MechanismsForm

Founder Voice-Discovery Interview

A questionnaire the founder answers in their own words (voice notes are fine) so posts, sessions and emails are built from real stories and real opinions.

Best example for: The first week of any engagement where content will be written as the founder and must not sound generic

S1 · TrafficBlogAll MechanismsPostOne or two a month; each spawns a post and a carousel

Best example for: Technical or cost-driven categories where the buyer searches for a problem they can't yet see on their own dashboards

Event-Platform Registration Page Description

Turn the plain text box on the event platform's registration page into a page that sells the seat: timing hook, diagnosis, what you'll learn, who it's for.

S2 · Landing + RegistrationLanding Pages & FormsAll MechanismsForm

Exit-Intent Popup

Catch the visitor on the way out with one proof line and a two-field form, so leaving takes one more decision.

S2 · Landing + RegistrationLanding Pages & FormsLive Session · ChallengePage

Event Terms and Conditions Page

Give the consent checkbox something real to point to: who can register, what the access link allows, who owns the content, how data is used, and what happens if the event moves.

Best example for: Any free live event whose registration form has a consent checkbox that links to terms, and whose content you want to protect from recording and resale

Best example for: Technical or sceptical buyers who resent demo gates, reached by cold ads or posts where the first click must cost them under a minute

Deliver a promised asset on WhatsApp the moment someone scans a QR code (on a slide, a page or a stand), and follow it with the one next step.

Best example for: Live sessions and in-person events where the audience is holding a phone, and you want the asset delivered and a conversation opened in one scan

One comparison slide that shows three ways to work with you, side by side, with seat caps and a deadline, so the buyer chooses between options, not between yes and no.

Deterministic rules that place every registrant into exactly one post-event track.

Funnel Analysis / Retro

The post-event review that turns one run into the next run's changes.

S5 · Revenue PipelineWhatsApp & SMSAll MechanismsSequence0h · 24h · 48h · 72h after the session

Post-session WhatsApp Follow-Ups, One Case Study per Message

Four WhatsApp messages across 72 hours that each carry one case study on an image card, so every touch answers a different objection before repeating the call CTA.

Best example for: Service offers where the buyer's objection is 'that won't work for a business like mine' and a named-type case answers it

S5 · Revenue PipelineWhatsApp & SMSAll MechanismsSequence0h · 24h · 48h · 72h

Post-session SMS Follow-Up Set

Four texts, each under 160 characters, that deliver the resources, the replay, a feedback question and a clean last call.

Best example for: Registrants who gave a phone number and ignore email; the shortest possible nudge to the replay and the call

S5 · Revenue PipelineEmail NurtureAll MechanismsEmailT+1d, or the same evening for an evening session

Attendee Offer Email With the Price Stated

One plain email to attendees that names the programme, states the price, and gives two doors: apply directly or book a short call first.

Best example for: Priced programmes and cohorts where stating the price up front filters out tyre-kickers and saves call time

S5 · Revenue PipelineEmail NurtureAll MechanismsSequenceE1 T+1d · E2 T+4d · E3 deadline −3d · E4 deadline −2d · E5 deadline −1d · E6 deadline +1d · E7 next intake −7d

Cohort Close Sequence (Primary Intake → Extension → Redirect)

Seven emails in three phases that run from the session to the intake deadline, extend once, then redirect everyone who did not apply to the next intake.

Best example for: Programmes sold in dated intakes, where a hard monthly deadline is the reason to decide now

S5 · Revenue PipelineLanding Pages & FormsAll MechanismsForm

Application Form With a Qualification Gate

The programme application: pre-filled from registration, three short sections, and a two-condition rule that routes each applicant to a Qualified or an Under-review branch.

Best example for: High-ticket offers where the buyer needs a qualification step before paying

S5 · Revenue PipelineLanding Pages & FormsLive Session · ChallengePage

Gated Replay Page

A short page that trades the recording for name, email, company and an optional LinkedIn URL, then plays it with the offer underneath.

Best example for: Recurring sessions where replay viewers are a second registration pool worth capturing with richer data

S5 · Revenue PipelineEmail NurtureAll MechanismsEmailT+0 (within an hour of the session ending)

Resource Delivery Email (Replay + Promised Bonuses)

Sent right after the session: the replay, every promised resource, a five-line recap and the single next step.

Best example for: Sessions that promised bonuses or templates live, where delivering them fast keeps the promise and reopens the call CTA

S5 · Revenue PipelineEmail NurtureLive Session · ChallengeSequenceT+1d · T+7d · T+14d · T+30d

No-Show Arc (Day After → 1 Week → 2 Weeks → 1 Month)

Four emails over a month that give no-shows the replay, the substance, a next live date and the same two doors attendees got.

Best example for: Recurring sessions with a large registered-but-absent pool that still fits the offer

S5 · Revenue PipelineFoundationsAll MechanismsOffer

Free Assessment Offer With a Pay-on-Adoption Pilot

A two-step offer: a free, no-obligation assessment that maps the buyer's top use cases, then a focused pilot the buyer pays for only if it meets KPIs agreed up front.

Best example for: Enterprise buyers who won't commit budget before seeing value, where a free assessment and a pilot paid on adoption remove the risk

S5 · Revenue PipelinePipeline & CRMAll MechanismsSchemaOne block of rows per run, filled within 48 hours

Per-Run Session Analytics Sheet

One tab, one row per run per source, carrying every count from invite to sale so each run can be compared with the last.

Best example for: Teams running the same session every few weeks who need one row per run and per source to see which channel actually produces buyers

S5 · Revenue PipelinePipeline & CRMAll MechanismsWorkflow

Automation Register

A single register of every automation in the funnel: its trigger, its action, the tool it runs in, its owner and its honest status.

Best example for: Any team with more than three automations, so everyone knows what fires, on what trigger, in which tool, and whether it's actually live

S5 · Revenue PipelinePipeline & CRMAll MechanismsSchema

The 11-Stage Deal Pipeline

One pipeline every mechanism shares: eleven stages, two exits, and the event that moves a contact into each one, so no stage is ever typed in by hand.

S5 · Revenue PipelinePipeline & CRMAll MechanismsSchema

Pipeline Fields and Tags

The exact field and tag names every guide, automation and report keys off. Rename one and something downstream silently breaks.

S5 · Revenue PipelinePipeline & CRMAll MechanismsSchemaOffsets as written above: minutes for recovery, hours for reminders, days for follow-ups.

Follow-Up Matrix for Every Stage

One row per stage: what fires automatically, what a human does, how fast, and where the contact goes when nothing happens.

Answer someone who asked a question, then get them booked while they're still warm.

Case Study One-Pager

Quarterly Positioning Refresh

Keep the company overview, personas, competitor list and titles current so the loop doesn't drift.

S6 · Post-event GrowthNewsletter & 52-WeekAll MechanismsWorkflowWeekly for 52 weeks; checkpoints at weeks 12, 26, 39, 52

52-Week Newsletter Roadmap (4 Phases × 6 Editorial Pillars)

Plan a full year of newsletters as one story: four buying-stage phases, six editorial pillars, and a CTA that gets firmer as the year goes on.

Best example for: Enterprise or considered sales where the buyer needs a year of trust-building before the first call

S6 · Post-event GrowthNewsletter & 52-WeekAll MechanismsEmailLast email of the series

Newsletter Series Closer: The Two-Door Email

Close a long series by being honest about what the reader can now do alone, what is hard, and giving two exits: do it yourself, or do it with you.

Best example for: Ending a teach-it-all newsletter series where the method is public and the paid offer is doing it for them

S6 · Post-event GrowthNewsletter & 52-WeekAll MechanismsEmailWeekly, or 2× weekly for a short step arc

Newsletter Step Email: One Module or Pillar per Send

The workhorse of the long nurture: one step of Mechanism name per email, framed as where things quietly break and what the discipline looks like.

Best example for: Teaching a named method or course curriculum one step at a time to people who didn't buy after the session

S6 · Post-event GrowthNewsletter & 52-WeekAll MechanismsEmailPenultimate or final email of the series

Newsletter Founder-Story Email (Case-Study Format)

Near the end of a series, tell the host's own story as a case study (who, problem, solution, phases, did it work) so the reader sees the method applied first to the person selling it.

Best example for: Founder-led offers where the host's own build story is the strongest proof the method works

S6 · Post-event GrowthEmail NurtureAll MechanismsEmailWithin 48 hours of the application decision

Declined-Applicant Downsell Email

Turn a 'not this cohort' decision into a sale of the lower-priced, self-paced version without making the applicant feel rejected.

Best example for: Application-gated cohorts or high-ticket programmes that turn away applicants who still want the material

S6 · Post-event GrowthEmail NurtureLive Session · ChallengeEmail2–5 days after the missed run; the next run should be within 1–2 weeks

Next-Run Re-invite for Registrants Who Missed It

Bring a registrant who missed a dated run back to the next live one, by showing what happened in the room they missed.

Best example for: Recurring live sessions where no-shows are re-invited to the next run instead of being sent a replay

S6 · Post-event GrowthLinkedIn OutreachAll MechanismsScriptDay 25 after connection accept; one send

LinkedIn Soft Revival DM (Day 25, Non-repliers)

One last, low-pressure touch that gives a silent connection an easy way back in: the next live session, with the recording as a fallback.

Best example for: Connections who accepted but never replied to a four-touch LinkedIn sequence

S6 · Post-event GrowthNewsletter & 52-WeekAll MechanismsWorkflowMonthly; reviewed quarterly

Monthly Run and Cohort Calendar (12 Months)

One table for the year: each live session date, the application deadline it feeds, and when that cohort starts, so every email, page and DM quotes the same dates.

Best example for: Programmes that sell a cohort with a monthly intake and need every date published a year ahead
